It then recognized commentary when it enacted 3553(b). It's recognized it again in the other statutes that are cited in our brief and that I mentioned here today. And it was operating against the backdrop of not only, as I just mentioned, Braxton and I think the important statement that the Court makes at page 348 but also the Court's own decisions, obviously, in Stinson and then a case like Buford in 2001 that makes clear that commentary is a way that the agent -- that the Commission can change the interpretation of a guideline.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Kavanaugh?

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: I'll tick through a couple things quickly if I can. Justice Barrett raised the question about what if the commentary's inconsistent with the guideline, and I read Stinson on 43 -- I just want to make sure this is consistent with your answer -- to say, in those circumstances, you go with the guideline when there's a flat inconsistency. Is that your understanding?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Yes, Your Honor.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Justice Kagan asked about Stinson, the Williams piece of Stinson, and then they go through the different potential analogies. When they come to Seminole Rock -- and this goes to your syllogism at the beginning -- the Court cautions at the beginning that the analogy is not precise, which suggests that you don't follow it for all it's worth. I'm just curious what you think "not precise" means there.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: So the Court, I think, explains that what it means by "not precise" is that the guidelines go through congressional review whereas, at that time --

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Exactly. They say the --

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: -- roles -- roles did not. I mean, that --

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Because Congress has a role in promulgating the guidelines is what the Court follows up with. So the analogy is -- is not perfect to begin with, the Seminole Rock analogy to Stinson, correct?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Yeah. I think the Court acknowledges that it's not a perfect analogy.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Okay. Third -- third --

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: So what we're working with here isn't Seminole Rock.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: That's good enough for that one. The third -- third one --

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: -- Congress, you -- you mentioned that Congress has amended the commentary directly a few times.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: I -- I -- that -- that is true, but I -- I just want to make clear --

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: That's true. That's all I need.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: -- that I misspoke briefly as to the two acts I mentioned beyond the PROTECT Act.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Right. Does that reflect -- what does that reflect about Congress's understanding of 1B1.7, if anything?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: I think it reflects that 1B1.7 essentially means exactly what we viewed it to -- we view it to mean and what Stinson viewed it to mean, which is that commentary does play an important role in the interpretation of the guidelines. Now I acknowledge, Justice Barrett, it says that it could result in an error, but I think that's just cabining that not every case of failure to follow commentary is going to result in an error.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Last -- last thing --

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: You otherwise reach the correct result.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Last thing about stability of the system, which Justice Alito has raised. And, you know, I came on the federal judiciary in 2006, a year after Booker and years and years of -- of trying to figure out how to apply that. I worry that if we change here, we're going to have years and years of trying to figure out how much weight you give to particular commentary and different courts going different ways. Your position, though, is not the same as -- as the amicus. If you're looking for stability and not changing, yours seems like it's also a solution in search of a problem as well. So why isn't amicus's approach in terms of stability, which may not be the overriding issue, but if it is an issue, stability's better served by amicus's position, not yours, correct?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: I -- yes, there would certainly be less upheaval under that. And as I mentioned to Justice Sotomayor, if the Court wants to go that way, I mean, frankly, in -- in -- in many policy respects, we'd prefer that approach. We're just working with what Kisor said and combining it with what Stinson said.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: We think that's the result that is reached under those precedents.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Barrett?

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Mr. Feigin, I just want to clarify your view of 1B1.7. Okay. So you said you think it's just sort of nomenclature that could be reversed on appeal if you -- if you don't follow the commentary to a guideline. Do you understand 1B1.7 to be the kind of express instruction from the Commission that I posited with Mr. Page saying, like, yes, this is a guideline that says you have to follow the commentary, or do you read it to mean not that strong?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: I think it comes pretty close, Your Honor, and I think Stinson largely reads it that way. It mentions 1B1.7 several times. Now it disregards the commentary to 1B1.7 at one point, but the text of 1B1.7 has been consistent, it's been congressionally reviewed multiple times. And I do think that it is the kind of express acknowledgment, first of all, that this is the type of thing the Commission's going to do and, second of all, the effect it's going to have because, of course, the analogy that's -- the -- the direct link between Williams and Stinson that Stinson draws is the -- on the 3742(f)(1) reversal for failure to correctly apply the guidelines issue. So I think that shows that what 1B1.7 is trying to do is give it the effect that Williams found it to have, which is essentially the effect of a policy statement.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Okay. So do you think it's fair to just consider -- there were questions earlier to Mr. Page about whether commentary should just be considered the same thing as a policy statement. What do you think about that?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: So I don't think it can quite be considered the same thing as a policy statement for a couple of reasons. One is 1B1.7 clearly does draw a distinction between the two. It may not be a substantive distinction in terms of how everything shakes out in practice, but it is at least a terminological distinction. And then, if we follow the Chenery Principle that an agency can't be kind of understood after the fact to do something that it didn't understand itself to be doing in the first instance, I don't think it's fair to say that when the Commission is issuing something that it labels as commentary and not a policy statement -- and I do agree with my friend that, you know, the fact that you can attach commentary to a policy statement makes it particularly strange to think that it is a policy statement -- that the Commission was actually issuing policy statements all the time.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Jackson?

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: So isn't your answer to Justice Gorsuch's questions about whether -- where the authority or delegation regarding the deference come from the Sentencing Reform Act? I mean, I thought the Sentencing Reform Act expressly created a binding system that removed sentencing authority from judges, their discretion in that regard, and gave it to the Commission. And at the time it was created, it was binding. Judges didn't -- they had to defer to the Commission's determinations initially. Is that the wrong way to look at it in terms of thinking about where this comes from?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: No, Your Honor. I mean, that was the original conception of the sentencing guidelines. I mean, they would give to the Commission the ability to prescribe ranges that were almost always going to be binding on the sentencing court.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: And also, general policy statements regarding application of the guidelines or any other aspect of the sentence or sentencing implementation. And I appreciate that there, afterwards, were developed something that the Commission called a "policy statement" as opposed to commentary describing the guidelines, but isn't Congress giving the Commission the authority to do all of that in the context of setting up a guidelines system?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: I think so, Your Honor. I think that -- I don't think that anything the Commission is doing is beyond its authority. And we think it's fine as it is. And we certainly think it would be fine if done as a -- if done as a policy statement.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: So you're just here because Kisor made a change and because Stinson referenced Kisor -- I mean referenced Seminole Rock as an analogy?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Well, we're not here because Kisor made a change insofar as Kisor just kind of explicated --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Reinterpreted Seminole Rock?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: -- what had always -- re- -- it, as it put it, you know, restated and expanded on what we understand to have always been the case.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: But I heard you say that you would be fine if the Court were to say that whole Kisor thing is really not for this area. We don't have to adopt Kisor in the government's position?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: That would be fine or a -- I mean, like, we don't think that's quite where the precedents lead, but if the Court wants to do that, I -- I -- I don't have any real push-back for you. I would say that one easy way to say that without really kind of discarding Kisor altogether would just be the approach that's suggested in our brief, which essentially says that although Kisor applies, it's basically going to shake out the way that people have always understood it essentially to shake out.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: No, I understand, but one -- one last question. How is Kisor consistent with Congress's broader goal of eliminating disparity? I mean, if our question is, do we adopt a Kisor-based approach or do we not for this area, why is it -- why -- why is it superior to do so --

turns.name: FEIGN
turns.text: Well --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: -- other than the fact that we made this reference in -- to Seminole Rock in Stinson?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: So, Your Honor, just being faithful to the statutes and to this Court's precedents, there is a difference between guideline text and commentary. Commentary does -- although, by practice, it's subjected to notice and comment, goes through congressional review, gets the vote of four commissioners, it doesn't have to. And so the guideline text needs to be there as an anchor, and the commentary is -- has to be anchored to the guideline text. And I think that to the extent courts would interpret commentary to be able to overrule guideline text or do things that the guideline text would think are unreasonable, if you agree -- to the extent the courts are reading Stinson deference to do that, I do think it's fair --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Which would be wrong -- in your -- in your dialogue with Justice Barrett, we determined that that would be a wrong way to interpret Stinson. But fine.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: I think there has -- to the extent -- I mean, I -- I understand there's a little bit of dancing on the head of a pin going on here, but I think clarifying that Stinson -- you can't take Stinson to actually mean what Kisor described as the caricature of just reflexive deference, that there are going -- there could, in theory, be these very isolated instances where the commentary goes too far.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: I understand.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: But -- yeah.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Thank you, counsel.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Mr. Dick. COURT-APPOINTED AMICUS CURIAE

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court: It is emphatically the province of the judiciary to say what the law is, but the advisory sentencing guidelines are not the law. They are advisory. As a result, when interpreting the guidelines, the question is not what the law is but, rather, what is the non-binding advice that the Commission is offering about what type of sentence should be imposed? On that question, the sensible approach is to defer to the Commission on the meaning of its own non-binding advice and then have courts decide for themselves, based on their own independent judgment, whether to follow that advice in deciding what type of sentence they want to impose. Now this type of deference doesn't pose any of the problems that you get when you defer to executive agencies on the meaning of the binding rules that they promulgate and enforce. That creates all kinds of problems for the separation of powers and the rule of law that this Court has cut back on in its recent decisions. But Congress gave us two very clear indications that the Commission is different from executive agencies when it comes to deference. First, Section 706 of the APA, which applies to executive agencies, makes very clear that courts should be the ones to resolve interpretive issues. So anytime you have an executive agency claiming authority for deference, that is a backdrop that's going to require a very clear statement to overcome. Second, instead of Section 706 of the APA, which does not apply to the Sentencing Commission at all, what we have is the text of the Sentencing Reform Act, which does authorize the Commission not only to promulgate guidelines but also to promulgate policy statements that authoritatively interpret the guidelines. And, Justice Gorsuch, that is the square holding of Williams, which we can talk about. In Williams, this Court held that when a policy statement interprets a guideline, that is an authoritative interpretation of the guideline. And then, in Stinson, this Court simply recognized that when the Commission uses the label of "commentary" to interpret a guideline, that falls within the same statutory authority. And Stinson starts with Williams, and it doesn't get to Seminole Rock until after it says that there is authority to interpret the guidelines. So, as a result of all of that, the Commission's deference that it gets is based on express statutory text. There's no need to rely here on any fictional presumption of implied delegation. This Court's cases cutting back on that fictional presumption in Loper Bright and Kisor simply don't apply. And the deference that the Commission enjoys rests on express authority that is just as sturdy today as it was when Stinson was decided. Stinson should be upheld. There's no reason to create the chaos that would come from overruling it. And I welcome the Court's questions.

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: Mr. Dick, this argument reminds me of my metaphysics class.

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: And that's not necessarily a compliment.

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: Let's go back to what this case is about so I can have an under -- a complete understanding of how we're looking -- what we're looking at. This is a provision that says -- that enhances the sentence for a large capacity magazine. That's the language, right? Where do we find that definition of what a large capacity magazine is?

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: In the commentary that defines it as a magazine capable of holding more than 15 rounds.

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: And if a judge disagrees with that and says, I don't think that a large capacity magazine is -- that that is a large capacity magazine, what is the effect?

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: Well, I think that the authority to interpret what that means has been given in the first instance to the Commission.

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: What is --

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: So judges --

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: -- what is the guideline based on then?

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: The guideline is based on the Commission's authority under 994(a)(1) to promulgate a guideline for the enhancement. And then the Commission has been given the authority to interpret that in the first instance through policy statements. And my submission is that it should not make any difference whether the Commission uses the label of "policy statement" or uses the label of "commentary" when it interprets that guideline. So I think it -- you know, you should think about it in two steps. First, has there been authority given to the Commission to interpret what that means? The answer to that is yes. That's Williams and Stinson. And then the second step is, okay, we have authority for the Commission to interpret the guideline. Now what we need to do at step 2 is to police whether the Commission has gone outside the boundaries of that delegated authority. That's what the Stinson test is for. If it's inconsistent with or a plainly erroneous interpretation, the Commission can't go there, but as long as you can put these two provisions together and sensibly read them together to determine what the Commission's non-binding advice is, if they can be reconciled, Your Honor, they should be read together to give the authoritative position on what sentence the Commission is recommending. Then, of course, it is up to the courts to exercise their independent discretion, do we want to follow that advice or not? But I think it would be nonsensical to try to interpret the guideline as a standalone statute as if it were something written like a statute that is going to have its own independent legal meaning when, in fact, it was promulgated with the commentary simultaneously to Congress, hey, here is what the guideline says, large capacity magazine, here is what large capacity magazine means. It's all part of the same package through notice and comment. And I think it's very, very different from a statute that's going to be freestanding and have some meaning --

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: The --

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: -- apart from that.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: -- the last step of that that you mentioned is important, I think. After you go through and determine the advisory guidelines range, you look at the guideline, you look at the commentary, you come up with the advisory guideline range. The court can decide -- the district court can decide to vary up, down, or stay within the guidelines range. So, ultimately, that's post-Booker, obviously. How does that fit into what you're talking about?

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: Absolutely right, Your Honor. I think so. Usually, you discard your precedents when they've been undermined or weakened. But, in this case, Booker has made Stinson a hundred times stronger because now the consequences of deferring are nothing like we get in the executive context, where you're talking about binding law that can have implications for fair notice and all kinds of other problems we get when an agency gets to promulgate, interpret, and enforce its own rules.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Now the counter to that would be that the advisory range still has some force and that some judges want to be guideline sentencers and some judges don't. So you have a disparity out there. But, for the judges who want to be guideline-centric sentencers --

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: Right.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: -- it still has some magnetic effect. So how do you deal with that?

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: Absolutely. I mean, I think the Court basically dealt with this in Beckles, where it said, yes, some judges may find the guidelines persuasive and may decide to follow them. But the point is it's ultimately the judge's decision. And if you look at the backdrop against the -- you know, the traditional system was Congress prescribes a crime. Congress prescribes the statutory range. And the judge could pick a sentence based on whatever characteristic the judge wants within that range. And that's not a fair notice problem. That's not any kind of separation-of-powers problem or rule-of-law problem. Much less going to be a problem when the Commission recommends a sentence within that range. And that's what makes this very different from all of the executive agency deference cases. You could think there's no legitimate agency difference ever and still think that deference is appropriate here because of the advisory nature of that.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Mr. Dick, that's -- it's -- it's a nice reconceptualization of Stinson, but that's not what Stinson said, I mean, and -- and you resist the government vehemently in your brief on -- on trying to Kisor this and saying we can't rely on implicit delegations, right, and that the ambiguity trigger isn't meaningful, right? You're shaking your head. I'm taking that as --

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: Correct, correct, Your Honor. Yeah, I think --

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: And -- and -- and -- and -- and -- and -- and so you say we just can't go down that road and also that Stinson suggests that even -- even unambiguous guidelines could be revised or glossed by -- by the -- by commentary, you know, in kind of a Brand X sort of way and override judicial opinions. And you reject all of those things that are associated with Stinson. And you try and ground it admirably in -- in statutory text and express delegation. But I'm having a hard time seeing that in 994. Yes, they have the authority to write these things. But all courts have to do is consider them under 3553, absent special circumstances, where courts are bound by them. Congress knows how to write that. Normally, we say that's a contextual clue that should give us some -- some idea that the other -- other situation's different, that the normal run of the situation is different. So I just don't see how that doesn't -- Mr. Feigin and his colleagues will be up here in the next case saying, hey, look at this statute, it's exact -- written exactly the same way and that agency too should be allowed to write binding regulations.

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: Absolutely, Your Honor. I think you're right to worry that the government is going to try to circumvent Loper Bright by trying to find an express delegation in every vaguely worded statute they can find. I'm very sensitive to that problem, and here is why I think it's not a problem. So, first of all, you've got Section 706, which is a very clear statutory command.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Forget about that. Forget -- forget about that here. Work -- work with the statute we have here.

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: Absolutely, Your Honor, but I think it's important to realize that in any executive context, you're going to have that statutory background rule of 706.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: We also have Article III in every case --

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: You do have Article III, but Loper Bright says --

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: -- which says that judges normally interpret law de novo.

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: Absolutely.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Right? You --

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: Absolutely. That's right. But Loper Bright says that when the Congress gives authority to an agency to promulgate something with binding effect, that -- then that is not an Article III problem. I think the problem, you know, in that type of situation may be a non-delegation problem. But -- but put that to the side.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: No, I'm not talking about that. Put that to the side is right. I -- I'm saying just look at the statute we have here. Where does it say -- where are there any words saying that the Sentencing Commission shall have something binding in --

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: Right.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: -- in -- in -- in -- in policy statements, let alone commentary?

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: So -- so let me address the -- the -- the text of the Sentencing Reform Act. So the first point about it is that Williams squarely held this, so you don't need to reinvent any new wheels here with respect to policy statements. But let me point you to the features of the text that I think are most important. So you've got Section 994(a) authorizing the promulgation of guidelines and policy statements as two prongs of the same authority that what it can promulgate, right, so I think both of those should be understood to be different types of authoritative statements. Then I would direct you to Section 995(b), which is the adjacent provision, which refers to "the power of the Commission" to "establish policy statements and guidelines."

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Yeah, it's --

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: So --

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: -- very similar to the Rules Enabling Act in the civil rules context, which says that the rules committee shall report to this Court and to Congress rules and -- and -- and -- and give explanatory notes. And nobody has ever thought that the advisory notes are -- are binding.

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: Yeah. It's absolutely nothing like the Rules Enabling Act or any other statute that we've been able to find regarding an executive agency. The Rules Enabling Act does not say that there is a power to issue or establish a statement that regards application of -- of the rules. I think that's just very, very different. So I think you have here text that is very unique in the Sentencing Reform Act that is not -- you don't have to read it against the backdrop of 706.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: I think it says may -- may provide explanatory notes, is what the statute says.

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: Well, it does not refer to a power -- the power, right, to promulgate something that -- and establish something on the same par as a guideline, and --

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Okay. But then every -- every administrative agency has the power to issue interpretive regulations, the power --

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: Not -- not in a statute -- not in a statute that says you have the power to issue and establish a statement regarding application of this. Even if you did have that with an administrative agency, you'd have to deal with whether that is a clear enough statement to overcome Section 706.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: What -- and what --

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: Here, you don't have to.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: -- what about the topsy-turvy problem that we have binding commentary --

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: Oh.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: -- advisory guidelines?

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: Not a problem at all.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: And -- and I know you say this is all good with Booker, but, boy, the more -- the more you make these things binding, you're creeping up to a Booker problem again.

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: It's -- it's binding only in the sense of it's what the Commission's advice means.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Yeah, but --

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: It's binding on the meaning of the guideline, not binding in the sense you have to follow it.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: You agree all these guidelines have heavy gravitational force in sentencing in America?

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: Exactly.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: That they're --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: And isn't that the point of the Sentencing Reform Act? I mean, again, I guess I don't understand how the system works unless it is binding. If -- if the whole point of this is to have the gravitational pull that comes from judges all starting at the same advice from the Commission --

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: Well --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: -- I don't understand how we're going to have a guidelines system unless you have judges calculating this consistent with what the Commission says to do.

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: Exactly right. So, you know, Congress initially wanted it to be binding in the sense that courts would have to follow it. Now it's not binding, but I agree with you it still does have a significant anchoring effect. Nobody disputes that. I think that is a very good thing because it helps enhance consistency. And one of the main reasons that we get that consistency is because, up until recently, everyone has understood we'll follow the same commentary to get the same meaning of what the Commission is advising. So it's still --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: And, right now, that's the starting point, so fine, everybody has the same starting point. But, in -- in direct answer to Justice Thomas, I would think you would say a judge who disagrees that the enhancement should apply for a large capacity magazine in this situation would just vary at the end of the day.

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: Correct.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Right.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Also --

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: So I think that it confirms --

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: I'm sorry, go ahead.

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: Mr. Chief Justice, please.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Loper Bright has been mentioned a few times, and it had a footnote that talked about express delegation, and you mentioned this, I think, in your response to Justice Gorsuch. What is your understanding of the scope of that in Footnote 5?

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: The scope of -- the scope of?

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: The reference in Footnote 5 to the express delegation.

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: Right. So I think the points, the Court's point, you'd know better than I, but -- but was just that when Congress actually indicates that it is giving authority to an agency to promulgate a statement with the force and effect of law, then, of course, the court's role is to simply interpret that statutory authority and -- and find out what the scope of authority that's been given to the agency is and follow that authority. So that's very different from the type of presumption of implied delegation that would just exist as a kind of brooding omnipresence in the sky where we're going to assume that anytime there's an ambiguity there has been a delegation to an agency to have interpretive authority. So I think how that's relevant here is, in 994(a)(2), you have Congress saying that a -- the Commission can issue a statement regarding application of the guidelines and you have to just look at that statutory authority and interpret, okay, when is the agency, when is the Commission, acting within the scope of that authorization? And the answer is interpreting a guideline is part and parcel of the power to apply the guideline because, if you don't interpret the guideline to know what it means, you can't know how it applies. So the -- the question in the case is, what is the legitimate bounds of that power of interpretation? As long as the agency, the Commission, is doing what Stinson says, you're not plainly inconsistent or plainly erroneously interpreting the guideline, you're within the realm of -- of authority that Congress has conferred on what the Commission can do, and -- and that is subsidiary, of course, to the guidelines because the guidelines have to go through the full two-track process of notice and comment and congressional review. So, if the Commission wants to change the fundamental architecture, say something inconsistent with the guidelines, it would have to go through that process. But, if it just wants to exercise the delegated power to interpret the guidelines within the range of meanings that the guidelines can bear, it can use the policy statement process to do that. And it can call a policy statement commentary. I, for the life of me, cannot understand why the substantive authority of the Commission would suddenly vanish if it relabels a policy statement as commentary.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Well, Mr. Dick, Mr. Feigin said that would be a Chenery problem. Do you want to respond to that?

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: Yeah, I think it's completely different from Chenery. This is not an administrative context. This not an adjudication on the record. There's no obligation for the Commission to identify this is the basis for our rationale as if that were going to be subject to some sort of APA arbitrary-and-capricious review. What we have here instead is just a statutory authority given to the Commission to promulgate the guidelines based on the authority given in 994(a)(1) and (a)(2). And the question is, has what the Commission has promulgated fallen within the authority given to the agency? So you -- the sensible thing to do is look at what is the substantive authority given to the Commission. It's to promulgate guidelines, and then it's to promulgate statements --

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: But it seems to understand itself to be doing something different when it adopts commentary than when it adopts a policy statement because it calls them different things.

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: I don't think it's -- it understands itself to be exercising a different authority. I think what happened is that the Commission adopted these labels for purposes of readability and for purposes of making the manual more understandable. I mean, if you look back at the way that this worked, when the Sentencing Reform Act was first passed, it didn't refer to commentary at all. It referred to guidelines and policy statements. And the Commission promulgated a Guidelines Manual where it used different labels within that manual, and it said here's the whole thing promulgated under our 994(a) authority. And it's -- from very early on, it has been express in saying that 994(a) is the authority under which we're promulgating all of this, right? So I think the fact that it has chosen to use a different label for formatting purposes does not say anything about what authority the Commission understood itself to be acting under.

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: Well, only for formatting purposes, or is there, in fact, an understanding that the Commission has that these two things are slightly different? Like, when you're -- when you look at the -- at the manual as a whole and you try to figure out why they labeled one thing a policy statement and why they labeled another thing a commentary, what do you take?

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: Yeah, I think, frankly, there are overlapping instances where they sometimes use them for -- for the same and for different purposes. But I think, you know, the -- it's a Commission-created label that comes from the Commission. So Congress had never used the term "commentary" at all. And I think it's really, really important to understand the statutory history of how this worked because, in 3553(b), it used to be the case before Booker that courts were not allowed to depart unless they could identify some circumstance that had not been adequately taken account of by the Commission. So, after the Commission had created the Guidelines Manual and created a section of the Guidelines Manual called Commentary and created that term, the way that that term came about in the statute was the Commission goes to Congress and says, we are worried that we're going to start getting subpoenaed and we're going to start getting discovery about why and what -- you know, what we took into account in promulgating the Guidelines Manual. And so Congress, to solve that problem, then amends the Sentencing Reform Act, and what it does is it says, when you're considering what the Commission took into account, by the way, you can only look at the Guidelines Manual. And it then uses the label of "commentary" to say you can look at the policy statements, you can look at the guidelines, and you can look at the commentary, which is a Commission-created label. And it's acting just for the very narrow purpose of saying what you can look at in determining whether the Commission took something into account. So -- so Congress was just acting in a world where the Commission had created this section of the manual, and it wanted to tell people what they could look at. Congress was not saying anything at all about what authority these provisions were promulgated under. And I think the -- the really important thing about that is, when the -- when the Sentencing Reform Act was first passed with 994(a) as the only authority, the Commission used that authority to promulgate guidelines, policy statements, and commentary, which, to me, is very, very telling that it was relying on that authority as it had been created to issue commentary as a type of policy statement.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Thank you, counsel. Justice Thomas?

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: Mr. Dick, if Congress passed a statute that enhanced a sentence for possession of a large capacity magazine and the Commission issued an opinion or commentary on that statute and the court -- would a court be able to interpret the statute differently?

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: Absolutely not. I don't think anybody suggests that the Commission has authority to issue a policy statement in --

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: No, no, I said "if" it issued its opinion as to what that statute meant, would a court have the authority to review that and interpret the statute differently?

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: Absolutely. A court's authority to interpret the statute exists independently of anything the Commission would --

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: So the -- the court would have more liberty to do that with a statute than it does with the guidelines?

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: Absolutely, because 994(a)(2) gives the Commission authority to interpret and apply guidelines but not statutes. So that express delegation does not extend to interpreting statutes.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Alito? Justice Sotomayor? Justice Kagan? Justice Gorsuch?

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Sorry to belabor the point, Mr. Dick.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: But, when I look at Footnote 5 in Loper Bright, it says that certain things are or are not to be done as defined by or as determined by or as delineated by an agency. And we say that's an express delegation. And I do see that in 3553(e), for example, which says that such sentence shall be imposed in accordance with the guidelines and policy statements. Put aside your problem with commentary not being in 994, okay? There it is. That's exactly the kind of thing that Footnote 5 had in mind. It doesn't have in mind a statutory direction to consider the guidelines and policy statements or commentary.

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: Right. So, Your Honor, I think that the word "consider" is the same thing that's used for both guidelines and policy statements. So I don't think you can get anything out of "consider" because what you have -- the thing that gives force to the guidelines is Section 3741 -- excuse me, 3742(f)(1), which says that you can vacate a sentence for incorrect application of the guidelines, which is exactly the language used in --

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Sure. That tells you what a court of appeals can do. But I'm talking about in the first instance when a district court's 3553(a) is considered.

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: Right. Consider both the guidelines and the policy statements.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Sure.

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: So -- so the -- the consideration requirement is not where the force comes from. What the force comes from is 994(a)(1) and (a)(2), which authorizes the agency to establish both guidelines and policy statements.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: To promulgate.

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: 995(b) calls that a power to establish those things.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Sure.

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: And this Court squarely held in Williams that when the Commission promulgates a policy statement that interprets a guideline, that is an authoritative guide to the meaning of the guideline. If I could just say a word about why that is the holding of Williams --

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: No, no, I -- I'm -- forget about Williams. I'm asking just on the statutory language.

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: Right. So I don't think I can do any better than what I've said, which is 990 --

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Okay. All right. That's fine. Thank you.

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: Thank you, Your Honor.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Kavanaugh?

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Quickly, your approach that you're recommending would not be pro-defendant or pro-government, correct, in -- in the sense that --

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: Absolutely.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: -- some of these -- some of the commentary is pro-defendant in certain cases and some is pro-government in certain cases, correct?

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: That -- that's right, Your Honor. I think it's notable that in both Stinson and Williams themselves, those were commentary provisions that helped the defendants, you know, in terms of giving a more lenient sentence.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Since Booker made the guidelines advisory, I gather you're saying just take full account of all the advice of the Commission, which includes the commentary?

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: That's right. That's right.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: And then, third, I -- I would be concerned if I end up agreeing with your position, I would be concerned about making sure that we do anything to -- to undermine Loper Bright or Kisor, and I would want to make that crystal-clear. Your advice on how to do that.

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: Absolutely. I think the two critical points are, again, Section 706, which applies to executive agency, says courts have to do interpretation. That's a very clear statement that we don't want to defer to executive agency interpretations. And you would need very, very clear language, maybe like something in Footnote 5 from Loper Bright, to overcome that. That doesn't apply at all in the context of the Sentencing Reform Act, so you don't need as clear of a statement to get an express delegation. And then what you have is the very unique language of the Sentencing Reform Act, which, again, 994(a)(1) and (a)(2). 995(b), which refers to the power of the Commission to establish, I think, is very, very strong language about giving an actual legal power to the Commission to establish an interpretation with legal effect. And I think, finally, that (a)(2) language about policy statements regarding application of the guidelines matches up very well with 3742(f)(1), which talks about vacating a sentence if it's based on an incorrect application of the guidelines, which everybody understands to refer to interpretation is part of that. So I think, if you put all those things together, what you can do is say there's a very, very, very, you know, statute-specific reason to find an express delegation here that's not going to be present in any executive agency case. So the government, despite all their very smart lawyers, are not going to be able to come up with a way to use this to locate express delegations for executive agencies, very narrow, the Sentencing Commission and the Sentencing Reform Act is a extraordinarily specific instance, and you should uphold Stinson on that basis without doing anything in the project of Loper Bright and Kisor to cut back on the fictional presumption of implied delegation.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Barrett? Justice Jackson?

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: And so you're reading 3553 to say that Congress wanted courts to consider the Commission's recommendation, is that right, I mean, in other words, and the recommendation comes in the form of the guidelines, calculated as the Commission would have them?

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: Correct.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: So the deference here, the -- the binding nature of it is just in determining what the Commission's recommendation is. It's almost as if the Commission -- you know, I thought of this hypothetical, right? The Commission writes a letter to each judge in every sentencing circumstance and says: Here's our recommendation as to what you should do. Instead of doing that, we just have a guidelines system where the judge is supposed to determine what the Commission's recommendation is, but there really isn't room for the judge to exercise their discretion. They're just trying to figure out what the Commission recommended, right?

turns.name: ANTHONY J. DICK
turns.text: Exactly right. I think it's binding on what the Commission's advice means. It's not binding in the sense that courts have to follow it. That's exactly right.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Thank you, counsel. Mr. Page, rebuttal?

turns.name: KEVIN JOEL PAGE
turns.text: May it please the Court: The most workable regime is one of no deference because it eliminates all threshold tests before courts are required to calculate the guidelines. It is -- it remains a statutory command of what is left of Booker to calculate the guidelines. And so the Court should simply instruct the district courts to do that without asking them to decide whether the commentary is in tension with that or, if so, how much tension. It is also the case that if the Court were to scour the text of the Sentencing Reform Act, it will find no provision that states that -- that commentary or policy statements ought to bind the courts in the interpretation of the guidelines. And I do believe that -- that if the Court finds an express delegation of interpretive authority here, it will find them all over the place. 553(b) expressly authorizes the creation of interpretative rules. If there is an express delegation to make that bind -- to make the commentary binding, why not those as well? But I do want to -- to point out that I think, if the Court applies the limitations in Kisor to the commentary in the policy statements, that will actually solve many of the concerns that have been raised here today. It will resolve the -- one concern about disuniformity in the precedent because the -- the policy statements and the commentary will be available to resolve cases of grave ambiguity. It will resolve the -- any concerns the Court may have about stare decisis because the Court wouldn't be doing anything in the sentencing context to move from Stinson to Kisor that it didn't do in the agency context to go from Seminole Rock to Kisor. And if Williams pertains, it -- and I don't think a move to Kisor would undermine Williams in any way because, if Williams pertains to the interpretation of guidelines through policy statements, then there isn't any reason that Kisor wouldn't apply to that as well. As to the concern about whether or not moving to Kisor would open the floodgates to a number of resentencings, first of all, there are only a few cases of -- of tension between commentary and -- and the text of a guideline that have actually been litigated in this case, so I don't think that we can say that -- that every defendant will have an opportunity to challenge their guideline -- that it has arisen in 2B1.1, it has arisen in -- in this case, and it has arisen in 4B1.2, and there has been one issue about the -- the -- the issue of what a dangerous weapon is, but there has not been a floodgate of people asserting, even in a world where Kisor might be thought to apply to the guidelines, that their guideline calculations are infirm. And we can take, I think, my friend at his word and at his analysis that -- that Kisor would limit the amount of resentencing litigation that would happen or at least the amount of resentencings as well. Thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Thank you, counsel. Mr. Dick, this Court appointed you to brief and argue this case as an amicus curiae in support of the judgment below. You have ably discharged that responsibility, for which we are grateful. The case is submitted.
